title: Where the Weather Sends You
short: Out the window is Souda Bay, about 15 km long and one of the deepest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, with the Akrotiri peninsula sheltering it from the north. Today's detour from Mykonos is nothing new: ships have come here when the wind said so for centuries. In 1645, when Chania surrendered, townspeople who chose to leave were ferried across to the Venetian fort on the islet in the bay, which held out until 1715. On the shore lies the Commonwealth war cemetery, where families chose the words on the stones. Today warships sit across the water. Your shuttle sets down by the Market Hall, about 25 minutes away.
long:
Look out at the water first. Souda Bay is about 15 km long, usually described as one of the largest and deepest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, and the long arm of the Akrotiri peninsula to the north keeps most of the sea out of it. That is why Scarlet Lady is here. The wind closed Mykonos to you this morning, and a ship in trouble with the weather has been coming to this bay for as long as there have been ships. Chania itself is 7 km along the coast.

Find the small island near the mouth of the bay. Venice fortified it, with the main works usually dated to the 1570s, because whoever held it controlled the way in. Now think about a day in August 1645. The Ottomans had taken Chania after a siege of 56 days, and under the surrender terms the Venetian garrison and any townspeople who wished to leave were evacuated, unharmed, to Souda. Picture what that means for a household: a few hours to decide whether you stay in the house your family has lived in, under new masters, or leave it, and then the choosing of what fits in a boat. Some of those families had been in Chania since the 1250s, when the Venetians founded the town. Chania fell; the island did not. Souda, Gramvousa and Spinalonga stayed Venetian even after Candia surrendered in 1669, and Souda held until 1715, 70 years after the city behind it. Later, under the Ottomans, the same rock gave shelter to Cretan insurgents. For the ordinary people of the coast, an island fortress was part of the landscape of choices: a place to be sent, a place to run to.

Today a different set of workers uses the same depth of water. Look across the bay and you will see grey warships: Souda Bay hosts Greek naval facilities, a US naval support base and a NATO pier, with a NATO missile firing range up on Akrotiri. A bay that was a refuge for Venetian galleys is a refuge for the alliance's navies now.

The other thing on this shore is quieter. About 1.5 km from the port, by the water, is Souda Bay War Cemetery, run by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, with 1,564 burials. The Battle of Crete lasted from 20 May to 1 June 1941, and it was the first invasion in history carried out mainly from the air; the decisive point was Maleme airfield, west of Chania. The graves here are mostly British (862), then New Zealand (446) and Australian (197), with a few South African, Canadian and Indian burials. Many of the graves are unidentified. Where the name is known, there is often a line of personal inscription at the foot of the stone, and those words were chosen by families a very long way from here. If you are drawn to read them, that is the household history of this bay: farm boys from Otago and Queensland and clerks from London, and the people at home who had to decide what a stone should say in a few lines.

Crete's civilians were part of that battle too. The Maritime Museum later today has a gallery on 1941 that is about villagers as much as soldiers, and the tales of Cretan families fighting the paratroopers with whatever they had are well known on the island.

One more small thing before you land. Greek myth gave Crete a bronze guardian, Talos, who circled the island three times a day and stoned any strange ship that came near. The poem that tells it was written by Apollonius of Rhodes, so he links to the island you toured two days ago. Today the strange ships are allowed in, and the harbour is better for it. The shuttle (or the number 13 bus) takes about 25 minutes and will put you down near the Market Hall, the big cross-shaped building with its doors shut for restoration. That is your next stop.

title: One Roof, Every Trade
short: This cross-shaped hall is Chania's Municipal Market, begun in 1911 and, reportedly, modelled on Marseille's covered market. It stands on the stump of a Venetian bastion called Piatta Forma, so the town's shopping floor replaced a defence. Prime Minister Venizelos opened it on 4 December 1913, three days after Crete united with Greece. Four wings, 76 shops, and traditionally butchers, fishmongers, greengrocers and cheese and herb sellers under one roof. It is closed for restoration today (reopening announced for 4 December 2026), so look from outside, then walk north-east about 7 minutes to Splantzia.
long:
You are standing at a building with its doors shut, and that is fine; the outside tells most of the story. The Municipal Market is a cross, with four wings and an entrance facing each point of the compass, 76 shops grouped around the arms. Building began in 1911, and several tourism sources say the plan was modelled on the covered market of Marseille, which I would treat as a repeated claim rather than a proven one. It is closed for restoration, with its reopening announced for 4 December 2026, so you are seeing the shell of a place that is normally loud.

Start with what is underneath. The hall stands on the remains of a Venetian bastion called Piatta Forma, part of the line of walls on the eastern side of the city. To make room, part of the walls were demolished, one piece of the early 20th century's clearing of the old defences as the town outgrew them. That is a fine fact for a household historian: the wall that kept 16th-century families in was removed so that 20th-century families could shop. Behind the walls the town was cramped. Outside them there was space for a building with air, light and running water, which in those years counted as civic virtue. A single hall with standard stalls replaced scattered street markets, and the idea was public hygiene and civic pride in a brand-new Greek town.

The timing matters. The Greek flag went up at Firkas on 1 December 1913, the formal moment of Crete's union with Greece, and three days later Eleftherios Venizelos, who was born just outside Chania and by then was Prime Minister of Greece, came home to open the market. Whatever else it was, a covered market was a statement: this was now a modern city in a Greek state. A household in 1913 had changed flags without moving house. The people who bought bread, cheese and fish here had been Ottoman subjects, then residents of an autonomous Cretan State under four Great Powers for 15 years, and were now Greek citizens.

Think about what a market is for in a household. The wings were traditionally divided by trade: butchers, fishmongers, greengrocers, and sellers of cheese and herbs. Which wing held which trade is not recorded in anything easy to check, so take the layout loosely. But the principle is the point. Someone from each household walked the arms of the cross with a basket, knowing which stall had good mizithra (the soft fresh cheese that goes on dakos, the barley rusk with tomato), and who would weigh fairly. Crete's food has always depended on that kind of knowledge: wild greens (horta) from the hills, olive oil from the family trees, snails after rain, cheese pies called kalitsounia. When you eat later, you will see how much of it does not come from a shop at all.

Now stand back and use this spot to set up the layers of the town, because everything else today stacks on them. Under the hill ahead of you, Kastelli, lies Minoan Kydonia. Then came Greek and Roman Kydonia (the Romans took Crete in 69 BC). Then Byzantine rule, interrupted by the Arab Emirate of Crete from 824 to 961, when Nikephoros Phokas took the island back. In 1252 Venetian colonists founded La Canea on the old site, and Venice held it until 1645, when the Ottomans took the city after 56 days. Ottoman rule lasted until 1898, with a short Egyptian interlude from the 1830s to 1840. Then came the Cretan State, with Chania as its capital, from 1898 to 1913, and then Greece. Each change in that list altered something for a different group: who paid which tax, which building was a church and which a mosque, who could own land near the harbour, who had to leave. The rest of the morning is about those changes seen through ordinary lives.

If the wind is strong, you will feel it funnel along the street here. Keep going. Walk north-east, with the sea on your left and the old town on your right, for about 7 minutes to Splantzia, a square with a plane tree and, on its church, both a minaret and a bell tower. Coffee is waiting under the tree, and so is the story of what happened to a quarter of the city in 1923.

title: A Minaret and a Bell
short: You are in Plateia 1821, Splantzia, the old Muslim quarter. The church in front of you, Agios Nikolaos, was built around 1320 by Dominican friars, became the Sultan's mosque after 1645, and has been Orthodox again since 1918. It wears a minaret (about 36 m) and a bell tower added in the 1950s, reportedly a combination found nowhere else in Greece. Neighbours here spoke the same Greek and prayed in different buildings, until the 1923 population exchange sent the Muslim families away. The big plane tree has a hanging story that is legend. Coffee at Platanos, then 4 minutes west, uphill, to Kastelli.
long:
You are in Plateia 1821, in the district called Splantzia, from the Venetian word for piazza. The big plane tree is in front of you, tables for coffee are under it, and across the square stands a church with a tall round minaret next to a bell tower. That odd pairing is the whole story of the neighbourhood in one building.

The church is Agios Nikolaos. Dominican friars built it around 1320 as a Roman Catholic monastery church, in the Venetian period, when the Dominicans of Candia ran a brotherhood here. After the Ottomans took the city in 1645, it was one of three churches converted into mosques right away, and it became the Hünkar Camii, the Sultan's Mosque, named for Sultan Ibrahim, who had launched the war. The cylindrical minaret is about 36 m tall, and with its lost conical cap it would have topped 40. In 1918 it was reconsecrated as an Orthodox church dedicated to St Nicholas. The bell tower was added in the 1950s. It is often called the only building in Greece with both a minaret and a bell tower; that is widely repeated rather than proven. Today it is a working church, usually open in the daytime outside services, free to enter, and worth a quiet look if you are dressed for it.

Now think of the square on an ordinary morning in, say, the 18th century. Splantzia was the heart of the Muslim quarter; Topanas, to the west, was the Christian quarter, and the Jewish quarter, Evraiki, lay near it, a few streets away. But the labels flatter the neatness. Many of the Muslims here were Cretans whose families had converted over the generations after 1645, and they spoke Greek. They ate the same food, followed the same seasons, and heard the same music as their Christian neighbours. The difference was which building they entered on Friday or on Sunday, what taxes they paid, and what the law allowed them. A tradition says the small church of Agioi Anargyroi, just off the square, was the only place Orthodox Christians were allowed to worship in the city; that is a tradition, not a checked fact, so hold it loosely. What the pattern suggests is how life under a conquering faith got organised day to day: you negotiated it. Households found workable arrangements with the neighbours on both sides of the wall.

The plane tree has its own tale, and it needs a warning label. Local tradition says Ottoman authorities hanged Orthodox clergy and rebels from it, and that the bishop of Kissamos, Melchisedek Despotakis, was hanged here in 1821. That is the sort of story that gets repeated because it feels right, and the record does not confirm it. Treat it as legend. What is solid is that 1821, the year the Greek revolution began, gave this square its name, and that Crete's part in that revolution brought reprisals and rebellion over and over, through the long chain of revolts in the 19th century.

Then comes 1923, the part for the quiet minute. Under the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece and Turkey exchanged populations by religion. Most Cretan Muslims left, many of them families who had lived here for generations and had never lived anywhere else, speaking Greek to the last. The houses were taken over by Orthodox refugees from Asia Minor, who were leaving their own homes and had also lost everything. Neither group had much choice, and both were households trying to start again with a few bags. When you look at the minaret, remember the community it was built for, here for centuries and then gone.

Platanos, on the square, is good for coffee or a raki under the tree, facing the church and minaret. After a meal in Crete, raki is often brought free, so the habit of hospitality has outlasted every change of flag. If the weather is turning, shelter under the tree's canopy for a minute or step into the church.

When you are ready, head about 4 minutes west, uphill, to Kastelli hill. Be ready for something much older: the layer under the layers, where a Bronze Age kitchen is waiting behind a fence.

title: The Kitchen Under the Hill
short: You are on Kastelli hill, over Minoan Kydonia. Through the fence at Agia Aikaterini square is a house from about 1450 BC, destroyed by fire. In its kitchen archaeologists found a clay hearth with a loom beside it and a jar of about 3 kg of burnt lentils and vetch. The fire baked clay tablets hard: about 99 Linear A accounts, plus sealings that locked jars and doors. A later Linear B tablet records honey for Zeus and Dionysos, a receipt for gods. The quince is named for the town. Walk down about 4 minutes to the Neoria on the east harbour.
long:
You are standing on top of a Bronze Age town. Kastelli hill, the low rise behind the harbour, has been lived on almost without a break for about 5,000 years; the one gap is roughly 1150 to 735 BC. Walk to Agia Aikaterini square, on Kanevaro Street, and look through the fence. Under a protective roof built in 2005 to 2008 is a patch of excavation about 600 m2 in area, with around 2 m of layers stacked up. Digs began in 1964, and from 1970 the Greek-Swedish excavation took over.

The house you are looking at is called Building 1. It covered 225 m2, had two storeys and 14 rooms on the ground floor, with streets and small squares around it. Now the detail I would walk a long way for. In a kitchen, archaeologists found a clay hearth with a loom beside it. In a jar there were about 3 kg of burnt legumes, vetch and lentils or peas, carbonised where they sat. Someone was cooking and weaving in the same room. Then, around 1450 BC, a fire swept through, part of a Crete-wide wave of destruction. The lentils never made it to dinner.

The fire left something else. Clay tablets, which would normally be dried in the sun and then crumble, were baked hard, so that about 97 to 99 Linear A tablets, found in 1973, survive from here, the second-largest archive of this script after Hagia Triada. Most are records of farm produce and livestock. Linear A has never been deciphered, so here is the oddity: we can read the numbers and some commodity signs, so we can read the accounts, but not the words. We can count the sheep and cannot say their names. Alongside the tablets were clay sealings, lumps pressed with a seal and stuck over the string on a jar, box or door, so that anyone could tell if it had been opened. One clay bar carries twelve impressions from ten different seals. That is bureaucracy in clay: someone checked who opened the storeroom.

The most famous find is the Master Impression, a sealing from the second half of the 15th century BC. It shows a long-haired male figure in a kilt, holding a staff or spear, standing over a multi-storey walled town on a rocky shore, with windows and horns of consecration on the buildings. The gold ring that made it has never been found. Scholars argue whether the figure is a ruler or a god, and whether the town is Kydonia; none of that can be proved. Note the walls: they sit awkwardly with the old idea of a peaceful Minoan Crete, itself contested.

Jump forward about two centuries. In 1989 and 1990 archaeologists found five Linear B tablets here, in the Greek of Mycenaean Crete, dated to the 13th century BC. One, called KH Gq 5, records honey. The reading is roughly: to the sanctuary of Zeus; to Zeus, honey, 1 amphora; to Dionysos, honey, 2 amphorae. Two later Greek gods, written together, with Dionysos getting double. That is religion as lived practice and as household economy: offerings budgeted on the same kind of clay as sheep and wool. (That it shows Dionysos already as Zeus's son is a guess, not a finding.)

Knossos is where the name of the town is securely written: Knossos scribes wrote ku-do-ni-ja in their records. No tablet found here has yet been shown to carry the name, so the safe claim is that Knossos knew this town. Inscribed jars from west Crete turned up at Thebes, traced by clay analysis. At Knossos, the tablets list named women as textile workers on rations; women clearly worked and took part in ritual. Whether they ruled is unknown, and the Minoan matriarchy of popular books is a modern idea, not a finding.

The town gave the world a fruit: the Greeks called the quince the Kydonian apple, and the botanical name Cydonia comes from it (a few linguists suspect an older word was bent to fit the town). Homer mentions the Kydonians, and the founder, King Kydon, is a myth with several versions. The Minotaur belongs to Knossos.

On top of all this the Byzantines built a wall in the 10th century and the Venetians made the hill their Castello, where nobles and officials lived, while Greek artisans and fishermen lived outside until the new walls of 1536 to 1568 enclosed them. Now go down, about 4 minutes, to the east harbour and the long stone sheds of the Neoria.

title: Sheds for the Winter Fleet
short: The long arched sheds along the south side are the Venetian Neoria, shipyards built from 1526 to 1599: 17 vaults here, five more (the Moro yards) on the east side, so about 22 in all, though some sources say 23. Each hall is about 50 m long, with an open sea end so galleys could be hauled in to be built, mended and kept dry for winter. In 1645 the Ottomans found 12 galleys inside. In a Moro yard sits Minoa, a lashed, nail-free replica of a Bronze Age ship rowed to Piraeus in 2004. The lighthouse is about 10 minutes out along the breakwater.
long:
Look at the row of long, arched stone sheds on the south side of the harbour. These are the Neoria, the Venetian shipyards, and they are one of the few places on this walk where you can see a whole working industry standing in front of you. The first two were finished in 1526. By 1593 there were 16, and the 17th completed the south range in 1599. A few years later five more, the Moro yards, were added on the east side of the harbour, where you are heading. That makes about 22 in all, though some sources say 23, and I would not pick one as certain. A row of seven vaulted halls survives together, with one more farther west, the Grand Arsenal, which now houses the Centre of Mediterranean Architecture.

The size is the point. Each hall was about 50 m long, 9 m wide and 10 m high, with arched openings in the side walls linking the halls, and the seaward end left open. Galleys could be hauled straight in on slipways. Inside, they were built, repaired, and kept through the winter, out of the storm season and safe from corsairs.

Who worked here? The sources are thin on names, so this is a reasonable inference and not a record: shipbuilding on this scale meant carpenters, caulkers, rope-makers and oarsmen, and a ship under repair needed people who could cut timber, drive and seal planks, spin and tar rope, and make sails. It was probably the town's biggest employer, and many families would have lived near it because of that.

When the city fell in 1645, the Ottomans walked into the arsenal and found 12 Venetian galleys sitting in the sheds. The building outlived its owners. Later uses reportedly included Ottoman and Egyptian military stores and then 20th-century warehouses and workshops, though the details are thin. Now a war factory is, in part, an architecture centre. It kept finding new work.

The Moro shipyard at the east end holds the thing I most want you to see. Minoa is an experimental replica of a Minoan ship of the 16th to 15th centuries BC, about 17 m long and about 4 m wide. It was built from 2001 to 2004 of split cypress planks lashed and sewn together, not nailed, with oars and a single square sail. The design drew on ship images such as the Akrotiri flotilla fresco on Santorini and on seals. In 2004 it was rowed and sailed some 210 nautical miles from Chania to Piraeus for the Athens Olympics, meeting the Olympic flame at the end. The annex is part of the Maritime Museum, entry about 3 euros, and open until 31 October; the Maritime Museum itself has its own hours and a separate ticket, and you will pass it later.

Stand next to a hull like that and think about the household around it. Someone has to cut the cypress, split the planks, make the rope that lashes them, weave the sail, and feed the crew who will row. And this is where an old Greek source gives us a line to hold lightly. Thucydides says Minos was the first to build a navy and that he cleared the sea of pirates so his revenues could come in. Whether there was ever a Minoan naval empire is argued over; scholars today tend to prefer the picture of trade and cultural influence. But the Minoan ships were real, the exported jars from this town turned up on the mainland, and the sea is the island's long constant.

If the weather is dry enough, now go out along the breakwater to the lighthouse, about 10 minutes away. The stones can be wet and slippery, and spray may come over; if so, skip it and take the view from the quay. The lighthouse looks a bit like a minaret, and there is a reason for that, which comes next.

title: The Tower at the Harbour Mouth
short: You are at the end of the breakwater, beside a tower with an octagonal base, a 16-sided middle and a round top. Someone has to tend a light like this, and the harbour behind you is the reason it exists: boats, cargo and fishing families all depended on getting in past these rocks. Venice built the first light here in the late 16th century. The tower you see was rebuilt in the 19th (local accounts say about 1839, under Egypt; other sources say 1864), and its shape is why people call it minaret-like. Look back at the waterfront: that is the working town, seen from the sea. If the spray is coming over, turn around here. Back along the breakwater and round the harbour, about 15 minutes, is the domed mosque.
long:
You are at the end of the breakwater, standing beside the lighthouse. Look up at the tower: an octagonal base, a 16-sided middle section and a round top, built of stone with a stair inside. If the sea is coming over the wall and the stones are wet, this is the moment to turn back, because the path here is uneven and nobody needs a photograph that badly. If it is safe, you are about 600 metres from where the breakwater begins, and you are standing in a place that exists for one reason: to get ordinary working boats home.

Think about who that meant. A harbour like this is not mostly about the grand ships. It is about the caique that left before dawn and has to find the gap between the rocks in a north wind, the cargo boat with oil or wine or cloth, the porter waiting on the quay, the customs man, the wife who watches the horizon from a kitchen window. A light is a promise made to all of them. Venice built the first one at the end of this breakwater in the late 16th century, usually dated 1595 to 1601. After the Ottoman conquest in 1645 it fell into neglect, which tells you something about priorities: when the flag changes, the soldiers and tax collectors arrive first and the maintenance budget comes later.

The tower you see is a 19th-century rebuild, and sources disagree on when. The most common local account puts it around 1839, during the ten years (1830 to 1840) when Crete was ruled from Egypt by Mehmet Ali, which is why it is sometimes called the Egyptian lighthouse. Other sources say 1864. I would hold both dates in your head and not choose. Either way it was built under a regime that was not Venetian and not yet Greek, and its octagon and stair gave it the look of a minaret. It is a good example of how a practical building quietly outlives the people who commissioned it.

The Egyptian decade itself is worth a sentence. It was short and odd: some tax reforms, some public works, a rebuilt lighthouse, and also unrest. For most households the question was the one it always is when rulers change: who collects the tax, and how much is left on the table. A fixed white light was installed in May 1915, making this an official lighthouse of the Greek service, two years after Crete joined Greece. Today it flashes red every 2.5 seconds, visible about 7 nautical miles out. It was damaged in the Second World War and restored in 2005 to 2006. Nothing I can point to names the keepers or harbour workers of any period, so I will not invent them; but a light like this needs someone to climb that stair, and that is worth picturing as you stand here.

There is an older kind of care on this coast, too. West of Chania, on the tip of the Rodopou peninsula, lies the sanctuary of Diktynna, whose name comes from the Greek word for a net. The legend says she threw herself from a cliff to escape King Minos and was caught in fishermen's nets, and became their goddess. That is a myth, and the sanctuary's oldest finds date only from the late 7th or 6th century BC, so it is not shown to be Minoan. But it is a lovely detail: a goddess whom fishing families prayed to, because the net was how they ate.

Now turn and look back. This is the best view of the whole waterfront, and what you are really seeing is the working street of the town: the quay, the mosque dome, the old shipyards, the houses stacked behind. For generations the walk out here has been a family ritual, an evening stroll along the sea wall. Notice who is walking it today, in whatever weather you have been given.

When you are ready, head back along the breakwater and then round the harbour. It is about 15 minutes along the quay to the low domed mosque, the next stop.

title: The Neighbours' Mosque by the Sea
short: The squat building with the big dome and a row of small domes over its porch is the Kioutsouk Hasan mosque, also called Yiali Tzamisi, the Seaside Mosque. It went up from 1645, right after the Ottoman conquest, and is usually called the oldest surviving Ottoman building on Crete. The minaret is gone. Imagine it as a neighbourhood fixture on the quay: prayer, coffee and trade within a few steps of each other. After 1923 it was a warehouse, a museum and a tourist office; now it opens only for exhibitions, so look for a sign. It is named for Küçük (Little) Hasan Pasha, the first Ottoman commander. Walk west along the harbour, about 5 minutes, to Firkas.
long:
You are standing in front of the Kioutsouk Hasan mosque, called Yiali Tzamisi by the Greeks, the Seaside Mosque. It has a large hemispherical dome on four great arches and a row of smaller domes over the porch (sources count six or seven, so count them yourself). There was a minaret; it was demolished in the 20th century, in the 1920s or by 1939 depending on whom you read. It opens only for temporary exhibitions, so check the door, but the building is the point from outside anyway.

It was built from 1645, straight after the Ottoman conquest, and is usually called the oldest surviving Ottoman building on Crete. Some sources say 1645 and others 1645 to 1649, and the name is Küçük, "Little", Hasan Pasha, given as the first Ottoman commander of the city. It is also known as the Mosque of the Janissaries. Tradition names an Armenian architect; treat that as a story rather than a record.

First, how the town got here. In 1644 the Knights of Malta captured an Ottoman ship, reportedly carrying a member of the Sultan's harem, and put in on Crete. Sultan Ibrahim blamed Venice. The Ottoman fleet left Istanbul on 30 April 1645, reached Chania in late June, and the siege lasted 56 days (some sources say 54 or 57), ending on 22 August. Roughly 50,000 men and 416 ships came against about 12,000 defenders, mostly local militia rather than professional soldiers. A commander named Blasio Zulian held the little fort on the islet offshore with 30 men and chose to blow it up with himself and them inside rather than surrender. The Venetian garrison, and townspeople who wished to leave, were evacuated unharmed to Souda. The war moved on to Candia (Heraklion), where it lasted about 21 years.

Now the part that matters for Jamie's way of looking: what a conquest means on an ordinary street. Straight after the surrender, three churches in Chania became mosques. Venetian families who could go, went. An Ottoman garrison of about 8,000 stayed, and a garrison is not just soldiers; it is bakers, boatmen, coffee sellers, tailors, women running households, children underfoot. A mosque built on the quay, where the Venetian galleys had once tied up, did several jobs at once. It was a place to pray five times a day, but also a landmark, a meeting point and a sign of who now ran the harbour. I should be honest: what survives is the building and its dates, not a record of daily life around it. But it is reasonable to picture the quay as a working street, with fishermen, porters, coffee houses and customs men within earshot of the call to prayer.

The population that used it was more mixed than the word "Ottoman" suggests. Over the following generations many Cretans converted, and Muslims in Chania were often Greek-speaking Cretans, living next to Orthodox Christians and a Jewish community in a quarter of their own. Splantzia, where you stood earlier, was the Muslim quarter; Topanas, where you are going, was the Christian one. They shared a language, a cuisine and a good deal of music, and prayed in different buildings. That ended abruptly in 1923. Under the population exchange following the Treaty of Lausanne, most Cretan Muslims left, and the mosques lost their congregations almost overnight.

What happened to this building afterwards reads like a list of the city's priorities. It became a warehouse, then the Archaeological Museum, then an office of the Greek Tourism Organisation. It now belongs to the Port Fund, and is used for exhibitions. A building that outlasts its original purpose usually survives because it is useful, and it has been useful to every regime since.

Stand with your back to the sea for a moment and look at the dome, then at the harbour, and then at the people walking past. Then continue west along the waterfront. It is about 5 minutes to Firkas, the fortress at the harbour's western mouth.

title: Barracks, Prison and a Flag
short: Before you is Firkas, the Venetian bastion at the western mouth of the harbour. Its name comes from the Turkish firka, barracks, and under the Ottomans it was a barracks and a prison: hundreds of men eating, sleeping and waiting inside these walls. On 1 December 1913 the Greek flag went up here for Crete's union with Greece. Today it holds the Maritime Museum of Crete (09:00 to 17:00, 4 euros), with Bronze Age ship models, Venetian galleys and a Battle of Crete gallery. Look for the caique tools and nets: that is a fishing family's living. From here walk about 5 minutes south into Topanas and the old Jewish quarter.
long:
You are at Firkas, the fortress at the west end of the harbour. It was built in 1620, next to the San Salvatore bastion at the north-west corner of the walls, to guard the harbour mouth. The name is the giveaway about what came next: firka is Turkish for barracks, and under the Ottomans this was a barracks and a prison. The museum inside, the Maritime Museum of Crete (open 09:00 to 17:00, 4 euros), was founded in 1973.

Picture the place in use. After 1645, about 8,000 soldiers were left to hold Chania, and they had to be housed, fed and kept in order somewhere. A garrison eats grain and meat and oil every day, wears out boots, needs water and fuel and bread. The same buildings held prisoners, and a prison, then as now, was a household of its own: someone had to feed the inmates, and in many places in the period that fell partly to their families, who came to the gate with bread. I cannot document that for Firkas, so treat it as the general pattern rather than a local fact. What I can say is that every flag that flew here relied on ordinary people to keep it supplied.

Then the long unravelling. The 19th century brought a run of Cretan revolts: 1866 to 1869 (remembered most for Arkadi monastery, near Rethymno, where defenders blew up their powder store rather than surrender), then 1878, 1889 and 1895 to 1897. In each, villages emptied. Women and children took shelter in monasteries, and families had a man up in the mountains. The 1878 Pact of Halepa gave Crete limited home rule, a rare case of a revolt leading to paperwork that actually changed how people were governed.

In 1898 the Great Powers (Britain, France, Russia and Italy) set up the autonomous Cretan State, with Chania as its capital. That is why the town had consuls and a prince: Prince George of Greece was High Commissioner, living in Halepa, the district east of the old town. Eleftherios Venizelos, born in 1864 at Mournies just outside Chania, was a local lawyer-politician who led the Theriso revolt in 1905 against Prince George's rule, and in 1910 went to Athens and became Prime Minister of Greece. A rebel turned prime minister is a good story, but the more useful point for a household is that his career shows what it took to change who made the rules.

The decisive date is 1 December 1913. Under the Treaty of London of 30 May 1913, the Ottoman Empire gave up its rights to Crete, and on this fortress the Greek flag was raised. King Constantine and Venizelos attended. Three days later, on 4 December, Venizelos opened the new Municipal Market, which you saw this morning. The order is telling: first the flag, then the shops. A fresh political identity needed a modern place to buy cheese and fish.

What changed for whom? For Orthodox families, the end of Ottoman rule meant an end to second-class status. For Cretan Muslims, it began the last years before the 1923 exchange. And for the city, the capital stayed here until 1971, when it moved to Heraklion.

Now go into the museum if the weather is bad, because that is what it is for. The Bronze Age room has models of Minoan ships and finds from underwater archaeology. Look for the Venetian galleys, and the section on traditional boatbuilding: caiques, nets, tools. These show how a fishing or boatbuilding family made a living, which is the daily reality under all the flags. The Battle of Crete gallery in particular is about civilians as much as soldiers, since Cretan villagers fought paratroopers with whatever they had. Entry is 4 euros, and it closes at 17:00.

When you come out, walk about 5 minutes south, away from the water, into Topanas. That was the Venetian nobles' quarter and later the Christian quarter, and just beyond it is the old Jewish quarter, Evraiki.

title: The Courtyard of Evraiki
short: You are in the lanes of Evraiki, the old Jewish quarter, at the Etz Hayyim synagogue on Parodos Kondylaki. It began as a Venetian church and became a synagogue in the 17th century, and a community prayed, studied and lived in these lanes for centuries beside Christian and Muslim neighbours. In May 1944 the Germans arrested Chania's Jews, about 250 to 275 people; on 9 June the ship carrying them, the Tanais, was sunk by a British submarine that did not know who was aboard. The building was restored and reopened in 1999. It is open until 15:00 today (4 euros, with a short tour). Photograph the building only, please. Lunch is two minutes away at Tamam.
long:
You are at Etz Hayyim, on Parodos Kondylaki, in the streets of Evraiki, the Jewish quarter of Chania. Please be quiet and unhurried here. It is open today until 15:00; entry is 4 euros, which includes a short tour with the staff, and they ask that you photograph the building only, with no selfies. I would take the tour if you can.

The building began as a church in the Venetian period and became a synagogue in the 17th century, after the Ottoman conquest. A Jewish community lived in this quarter under the Venetians and under the Ottomans. It was a Romaniote community, one of the Greek-speaking Jewish traditions, and its roots on Crete are described as going back to antiquity. I will keep to what is documented, and to what the place itself shows. A synagogue like this is not only a room for prayer; in a small quarter it is usually also where the community gathers for the big moments of life. Here, a courtyard, a garden and a mikveh, the ritual bath, are part of the place, which tells you it was a house of daily life as well as worship.

What is striking, and what the visit shows you, is how normal it was. For centuries Jewish families in Chania lived in a mixed town, a few streets away from Splantzia's Muslim quarter and Topanas's Christian one, trading in the same markets, speaking the same Greek, and keeping their own calendar of festivals.

On 29 May 1944, during the German occupation, soldiers rounded up the Jews of Chania, about 250 to 275 people. (Another account gives 276 arrested on 20 May; sources differ on the exact date and number.) They were taken by truck to Heraklion and put on board a ship, the Tanais, together with Greek hostages and resistance prisoners and Italian prisoners of war. On 9 June 1944 the British submarine HMS Vivid fired four torpedoes at about 2,400 yards. Two hit, and the ship sank in about 12 seconds, north-west of the islet of Dia. The crew of the Vivid did not know who was aboard. Estimates of the dead run from 425 to 1,000; about 265 of them were Cretan Jews. This ended Crete's Jewish community. The Tanais had been sunk once before, by the Luftwaffe in Souda Bay in May 1941, then raised and repaired. A memorial to the victims stands in Chania, and the town marks the anniversary each June.

After the war the synagogue was a ruin. It was restored in the late 1990s, with Nikos Stavroulakis leading the work, and reopened in 1999. It was attacked by arsonists on 5 and 16 January 2010; the second fire destroyed about 2,500 rare books and manuscripts. It was repaired again. Today the congregation is mostly non-Jewish, following Sephardic customs and having written its own Haggadah; in effect, people who live here look after a house of prayer whose own community is gone. In 2006, Queen Sofia of Spain and the former King Constantine II visited unannounced.

Look at the memorial plaque, if the guide shows it to you. It lists the deported families by name. In a day of cannon and flag, it is a reminder of what the other half of history looks like: not battles, but households, one by one.

Take a moment in the courtyard. Then lunch: Tamam, on Zambeliou, is about two minutes away, in a former hammam (Ottoman bath), with Cretan-Ottoman cooking indoors, which suits this weather. After lunch, take a taxi east to the Archaeological Museum at Chalepa. It is about a 25-minute walk, so a taxi is kinder in the rain.

title: The Ledger and the Hearth
short: This is the Archaeological Museum of Chania at Skra 15, Chalepa, open 08:00 to 20:00 (15 euros with audio guide). It opened in 2022, and its best pieces are small. Look for the Master Impression, a tiny clay sealing from Kastelli, and the tablets: Linear A accounts and a Linear B tablet recording honey for Zeus and Dionysos. Those are household and temple bookkeeping. Look too for the painted clay coffin from Armeni (a cemetery near Rethymno) and the everyday Minoan pottery. This is the thread of the whole day: people kept stores, counted them and fed their gods. Take a taxi back to Souda in time for the ship by 18:00.
long:
You are at the Archaeological Museum of Chania, at Skra 15 in Chalepa. It opened in April 2022, replacing the old museum in the Venetian church of San Francesco in the old town, and it is open 08:00 to 20:00, with entry at 15 euros including an audio guide. If you are wet and tired, you have chosen well. Check the floor plan as you arrive, since the rooms may be arranged differently from what I describe.

Start with the thing you stood above this morning: the Minoan town on Kastelli hill. The best pieces here are small, and almost all of them are about managing a household. Look for the sealings, lumps of clay stamped with a seal. They were pressed onto jar stoppers, boxes and doors, so that anyone opening a storeroom had to break the seal; the excavation turned up a clay bar bearing twelve seal impressions from ten different seals. That is bureaucracy in clay. And then look for the Master Impression itself: the tiny sealing, a few centimetres across, showing a tall figure over a walled, multi-storey town by the sea. The gold ring that made it has never been found. Whether the figure is a ruler, a god or a ruler shown as divine is argued over, and I would not pretend to settle it.

Then the tablets. Kydonia produced something like 97 to 99 Linear A tablets, the second-largest archive of that script after Hagia Triada, mostly records of farm produce and livestock. They survive because the fire around 1450 BC baked them hard. No one can read Linear A as language; we can read the numbers and some commodity signs, so we can follow the accounts without knowing the words. If it is on display, look also for the Linear B tablet recording honey: roughly "to Zeus, honey", one amphora, and "to Dionysos, honey", two. It is about 800 years older than classical Greek drama, and religion appears as a line in the household budget, written on the same kind of clay as sheep and wool. The idea that it proves Dionysos was already Zeus's son is an inference, and debated.

Think back to the kitchen you saw through the fence: a clay hearth with a loom right beside it, and a jar holding about 3 kilograms of burnt lentils and vetch. Put the three together and you have a household: the hearth, the cloth, and the clerk upstairs counting. In Linear B records from Knossos, textile workers appear by name, women and children among them, on ration lists. Women's work was real and measured. Whether women held political power is unknown; the "matriarchy" idea is a modern projection, not evidence.

Look for the larnakes, painted clay coffins. One is decorated with a hunting scene. It comes from a cemetery at Armeni, near Rethymno, not Chania, which is why I am telling you. They date to 1400 to 1200 BC. Look for pottery, too: the "Kydonia workshop" wares of the 13th century BC, and large inscribed stirrup jars, oil or wine jars painted in Linear B, which clay analysis traces to west Crete; some turned up at Thebes. A jar like that is the Bronze Age equivalent of a shipping label. Then find the later cities, Greek and Roman Kydonia. Layers are the point.

Chalepa itself is a final lesson. In the Cretan State, from 1898 to 1913, this eastern district was where consuls and the prince's court lived, and the Venizelos house is here. The old town's harbour had galleys, then a garrison; Chalepa had a tidy world of diplomats and lawyers' households. Every era arranged its people differently, and each left a ledger of sorts.

So the day closes where it began: with the people under the hill, who counted their oil, wove their wool and gave honey to the gods. The Venetians built their shipyards, the Ottomans their mosques, the town its market and its synagogue, and underneath them the same questions about storage, work and neighbours kept coming round.

To go home, a taxi from here to Souda is the easiest way to be back on the ship before 18:00. Allow plenty of time in the rain, and give yourself a margin.
